'''Richard Franklin Mirer''' (born March 19, 1970) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 12 seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]], winning [[Touchdown Club of Columbus#Kellen Moore Award|Quarterback of the Year]] in 1992. Mirer was selected [[List of second overall NFL draft picks|second overall]] by the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in the [[1993 NFL draft]].<ref name="nytimes2002">{{Cite news |date=March 24, 2002 |title=Quarterback Mirer Goes to Raiders |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/03/24/sports/plus-pro-football-quarterback-mirer-goes-to-raiders.html?ref=rick_mirer |access-date=August 23, 2010 |work=[[New York Times]]|agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref>

In his first season, Mirer set the rookie records for passing yards, attempts, and completions, earning him [[List of NFL Rookie of the Year awards#NFC winners (1970–1996)|UPI Rookie of the Year]]. Unable to duplicate his success, Mirer would leave the Seahawks after four seasons. He spent the remainder of his career with the [[Chicago Bears]], [[New York Jets]], [[San Francisco 49ers]], [[Oakland Raiders]], and [[Detroit Lions]], mostly as a backup.

'''Rickey Anderson Jackson''' (born March 20, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[New Orleans Saints]] (1981–1993) and the [[San Francisco 49ers]] (1994–1995). He led the team's [[Dome Patrol]] linebacker corps while playing with the Saints. In 1997, Jackson was inducted into the New Orleans Saints Hall of Fame.<ref>[http://www.neworleanssaints.com/team/history/hall-of-fame.html "Saints Hall of Fame Inductees"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303212325/http://www.neworleanssaints.com/team/history/hall-of-fame.html |date=March 3, 2016 }}, ''[[New Orleans Saints]]'', 1997.</ref> Jackson won a [[Super Bowl ring]] with the 49ers in [[Super Bowl XXIX]] one year before retiring. On February 7, 2010, Jackson was elected to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]], the same day his [[New Orleans Saints]] won [[Super Bowl XLIV]].

'''Richard Lamar Tuten''' (January 5, 1965 – June 13, 2017)  was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[punter (American football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily with the [[Seattle Seahawks]]. He punted the ball 108 times in 1992, tied for fourth-most in a season in NFL history.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nfl.com/history/randf/records/indiv/punting |title=Individual Records: Punting |website=[[NFL.com]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040224231201/http://www.nfl.com/history/randf/records/indiv/punting |archive-date=February 24, 2004 |access-date=July 20, 2012 }}</ref> In 1992, he punted for 4,760 yards with an average of 44.1 yards per punt. In 1994, the year he went to his only Pro Bowl, he punted the ball 91 times for 3,905 yards, an average of 42.9 yards per punt, and also scored a two-point conversion, the only scored points of his career. Tuten also received a [[Super Bowl ring|ring]] as a member of the [[1999 St. Louis Rams football team|St. Louis Rams]]' [[Super Bowl XXXIV|Super Bowl]] championship team. However, he did not play in the game itself due to injury.

While with the Seattle Seahawks in 1998, he won the designation as the league's strongest man pound-for-pound in ''[[Flex (magazine)|Flex]]'' magazine.

He has a daughter named Ryan, who married [[Buffalo Bills]] Kicker [[Tyler Bass]] on March 15, 2024, in Ocala, FL. He also has a son named Chase.

While on vacation with his wife in [[Costa Rica]] in <!--June 13,-->2017, Tuten unexpectedly died at age 52.<ref>{{cite web | last=Brand | first=Aaron | title=Former NFL punter, Forest grad Rick Tuten dies | website=Ocala StarBanner | date=2017-06-13 | url=https://www.ocala.com/story/sports/2017/06/13/former-nfl-punter-forest-grad-rick-tuten-dies/20600280007/ | access-date=2025-10-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url = http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/ocala/obituary.aspx?n=rick-tuten&pid=186170688&referrer=0&preview=false| title = RICK TUTEN Obituary (2017) - Ocala, FL| website = [[Legacy.com]]}}</ref>

'''Richard Robert Volk''' (born March 15, 1945) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Baltimore Colts]], [[New York Giants]], and [[Miami Dolphins]]. He retired with 38 career [[interception]]s and 13 [[fumble recoveries]], and totaled 574 yards on interception returns and 548 yards on [[punt return]]s.

Volk played [[college football]] for the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]] from 1964 to 1966 and was a member of the [[1964 Michigan Wolverines football team|1964 team]] that won the [[Big Ten Conference]] championship and defeated [[1964 Oregon State Beavers football team|Oregon State]] in the [[1965 Rose Bowl]]. He played as a [[defensive back]] for Michigan's defensive unit and as a [[Halfback (American football)|halfback]] and [[quarterback]] for the offensive unit.  Volk was also selected by the [[Sporting News]] as a first-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] in 1967. In 1989, he was inducted into the [[University of Michigan Athletic Hall of Honor]]; Volk and [[Ron Johnson (running back)|Ron Johnson]] were the first two football players from the 1960s to be so honored.

Volk went on to a successful 12-year career as a [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] in the [[National Football League]]. He played nine years with the [[History of the Indianapolis Colts#NFL Baltimore Colts|Baltimore Colts]] from 1967 to 1975. He was a member of the Colts' teams that lost [[Super Bowl III]] to the [[New York Jets]] and won [[Super Bowl V]] against the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. Volk was selected as an NFL All-Pro four times (1968–1971) and played in three [[Pro Bowl]]s (1967, 1969, 1971). After being released by the Colts in April 1976, Volk concluded his playing career with the [[New York Giants]] in 1976 and the [[Miami Dolphins]] from 1977 to 1978. In 1977, Volk was selected by Baltimore fans as a starter for the Colts' 25th anniversary team.

In {{NFL Year|1987}}, after being out of the sport for a year, he was signed by the [[Detroit Lions]] during the [[1987 NFL strike]], in which teams hired [[replacement player]]s. He appeared in one game with the team, a 19–16 win over the [[Green Bay Packers]], before being released.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/J/JohnRi22/gamelog/1987/|website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]|title=Rick Johnson 1987 Game Log}}</ref>
